Yesterday brought two contradictory reports about next year's iPhone: on one hand, it's being framed as the model marking the twentieth anniversary of the iPhone's launch; on the other, it's being described as the physical realisation of Apple's long-standing "a slab of glass" vision.

As for what we can actually expect, these reports have been going back and forth for a while, but yesterday's divergence was arguably the most dramatic so far…

The current state of play

Apple's former design chief Jony Ive has spoken on multiple occasions about his long-term vision of one day turning the iPhone into "a slab of glass"; even though Ive has left the company, the prevailing view remains that Apple has been steadily working towards this goal.

Although Apple typically doesn't mount large-scale celebrations for anniversaries, the industry consensus is that they want to realise this vision as close as possible to the iPhone's twentieth anniversary. This could involve embedding Face ID under the display, as well as hiding the front-facing camera beneath the screen.

However, we've already seen contradictory reports on these expectations. The original view was that this would be a standalone model, similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but more recent reports suggest the design would appear on next year's iPhone Pro models.

As for naming, it might be called the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple could also choose to skip a generation and name it the iPhone 20 to mark the anniversary.

Yesterday's contradictory reports

Things got even more muddled yesterday when an analyst claimed Apple had scrapped plans to launch an all-glass iPhone next year.

But Bloomberg's Mark Gurman immediately pushed back on that claim.

The more likely scenario

The key point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone isn't a single, fixed destination. What they plan to launch next year is just one step — or several steps — towards that sci-fi "slab of glass" vision.

The question isn't whether that goal can be achieved next year, but how far Apple will move in that direction. But whether it's one step or several, this will absolutely not be the last step in the evolution of the iPhone's design.

In fact, Gurman revealed that Apple has indeed moderated some of its expectations for next year.

The analysts at Jefferies likely received the same information, just a beat later, and mistook it for the whole plan being shelved.

My own expectation is that next year's design will be a major leap — comparable to the breakthrough of the iPhone X — but with further developments still to come over the following years. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will have a breakthrough significant enough to warrant being marked in some special way — such as being labelled a twentieth-anniversary edition iPhone (which I think is unlikely), being given a special name, or skipping a generation to be called the iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
